          DEFENDANT META PLATFORMS, INC.’S RESPONSE IN OPPOSITION TO
               PLAINTIFF’S MOTION FOR LEAVE TO FILE A SUR-REPLY


           Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc., (“Meta”) by and through its undersigned counsel, hereby

  respectfully opposes Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine’s Motion for Leave to File a Sur-Reply, Dkt.

  No. 43 (“Mot. for Leave”). In support of its response, Meta states the following:

     I.       Legal Standard

           Courts in this District have held that “sur-replies are highly disfavored, as they usually are

  a strategic effort by the nonmoving party to have the last word on the matter.” Trustees of Columbia

  Univ. in City of New York v. Symantec Corp., No. 3:12-cv-808, 2019 WL 13189619, at *2 (E.D.

  Va. Oct. 10, 2019) (cleaned up and internal quotations omitted). As Plaintiff concedes, “an

  opposing party may not submit a sur-reply simply because the movant used their reply brief to

  further support an argument made in their opening brief or to respond to new arguments in the

  opposing party ’s opposition.” Taylor v. Revature, LLC¸ No. 1:22-cv-1153-RDA-WBP, 2025 WL




                                                     1

  711961, at *4 (E.D. Va. Mar. 5, 2025) (internal quotations and punctuation omitted); See Mot. for

  Leave, at 2.

      II.      Argument

            Plaintiff seeks leave to file a sur-reply in response to Meta’s Motion to Dismiss the First

  Amended Complaint (“FAC”), Dkt. No. 21 (“Motion to Dismiss”), asserting that Meta’s Reply in

  Support of its Motion to Dismiss (Dkt. No. 39) (“Reply”) “introduced a new proposition,” namely

  that “Plaintiff has not identified any non-speculative opportunity for him to provide testimony.”

  Dkt. No. 43 at 3 (quoting Meta’s Reply in Support of its Motion to Dismiss). But Meta’s argument

  that Plaintiff failed to sufficiently allege a non-speculative opportunity for him to testify merely

  develops the argument Meta made in its Motion to Dismiss that Plaintiff failed to sufficiently allege

  injury under 42 U.S.C. § 1985(2). In its Motion to Dismiss, Meta expressly argued that Plaintiff

  failed to allege injury because “Plaintiff fails to plead any facts showing that the discovery actually

  impacted his ability to testify or pursue his claim.” See Dkt. No. 22 at 12 (emphasis added); see

  also id. at 2.

            In his opposition to Meta’s Motion to Dismiss (Dkt. No. 30) (“Opposition”), Plaintiff

  argued that, even if physical presence in court was required to state a claim for the “attending

  court” prong of Section 1985(2), such physical presence would “not dispose of the testimony

  branch,” apparently conceding that Plaintiff’s Section 1985(2) claim relies solely on “Plaintiff’s

  prospective-witness status.” Dkt. No. 30 at 20-21. In response, Meta’s Reply further developed

  Meta’s argument that the FAC fails to allege injury because the FAC includes no non-speculative

  allegations that Plaintiff would testify in any action. See Dkt No. 39 at 7. This is not a new argument

  raised in reply, but rather a further development of an argument made in Meta’s Motion to Dismiss

  in response to Plaintiff’s Opposition. Accordingly, a sur-reply would be improper. See Johnson v.



                                                     2

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD              Document 69        Filed 09/15/26      Page 3 of 5 PageID# 728




  Henrico Cnty. Bd. of Supervisors, No. 3:23-cv-679, 2025 WL 310122, at *1, n.3 (E.D. Va. Jan. 27,

  2025) (refusing to “consider Plaintiff’s Sur-Reply” where defendant’s reply “introduced no new

  arguments or new material for which a sur-reply would be warranted”).

             Additionally, Plaintiff’s proposed sur-reply simply reiterates allegations from the FAC,

  pointing to Plaintiff’s allegation that he “expected to testify under oath at deposition” in the

  underlying actions between Plaintiff and Meta and asserting that solely because of this alleged

  expectation, “Plaintiff was a prospective witness” in those actions. As Meta’s Motion to Dismiss

  and Reply point out, Plaintiff’s allegations that he may have testified at some point in the

  underlying actions do not identify any non-speculative opportunity to testify. This is particularly

  true given that, at the time the alleged letters at issue were sent, Plaintiff’s claims in the underlying

  actions had not even survived initial motions to dismiss testing the viability of his allegations.

      III.      Conclusion

             For the foregoing reasons, Meta respectfully requests that the Court deny Plaintiff’s Motion

  for Leave to File a Sur-reply.
